claim: Blood flow is a fundamental determinant of tissue CO2/H+.
source: Blood flow is a fundamental determinant of tissue CO2/H+, yet little is known regarding how regulation of vascular tone in chemoreceptor regions contributes to respiratory behavior.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the abstract.

claim: CO2/H+-vasoconstriction in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) supports chemoreception by a purinergic-dependent mechanism in rats.
source: Previously, we showed in rat that CO2/H+-vasoconstriction in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) supports chemoreception by a purinergic-dependent mechanism (Hawkins et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hawkins et al., 2017).

claim: CO2/H+ dilates arterioles in chemoreceptor regions other than the RTN in mice.
source: Here, we show in mice that CO2/H+ dilates arterioles in other chemoreceptor regions, thus demonstrating CO2/H+ vascular reactivity in the RTN is unique.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1C).

claim: CO2/H+ vascular reactivity in the RTN is unique compared to other chemoreceptor regions.
source: Here, we show in mice that CO2/H+ dilates arterioles in other chemoreceptor regions, thus demonstrating CO2/H+ vascular reactivity in the RTN is unique.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing RTN to other regions (Figure 1C).

claim: P2Y2 receptors in RTN smooth muscle cells are the substrate responsible for CO2/H+-induced vasoconstriction.
source: We also identify P2Y2 receptors in RTN smooth muscle cells as the substrate responsible for this response.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including pharmacology, genetics, and rescue experiments (Figures 1, 2, 4).

claim: Pharmacological blockade of P2Y2 receptors blunted the ventilatory response to CO2.
source: Specifically, pharmacological blockade or genetic deletion of P2Y2 from smooth muscle cells blunted the ventilatory response to CO2, and re-expression of P2Y2 receptors only in RTN smooth muscle cells fully rescued the CO2/H+ chemoreflex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of AR-C118925 on ventilation (Figure 2).

claim: Genetic deletion of P2Y2 from smooth muscle cells blunted the ventilatory response to CO2.
source: Specifically, pharmacological blockade or genetic deletion of P2Y2 from smooth muscle cells blunted the ventilatory response to CO2, and re-expression of P2Y2 receptors only in RTN smooth muscle cells fully rescued the CO2/H+ chemoreflex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from P2Y2 cKO mice (Figure 4).

claim: Re-expression of P2Y2 receptors only in RTN smooth muscle cells fully rescued the CO2/H+ chemoreflex.
source: Specifically, pharmacological blockade or genetic deletion of P2Y2 from smooth muscle cells blunted the ventilatory response to CO2, and re-expression of P2Y2 receptors only in RTN smooth muscle cells fully rescued the CO2/H+ chemoreflex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from viral rescue experiments (Figure 4).

claim: P2Y2 receptors in RTN smooth muscle cells are requisite determinants of respiratory chemoreception.
source: These results identify P2Y2 receptors in RTN smooth muscle cells as requisite determinants of respiratory chemoreception.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined results of knockout and rescue experiments (Figure 4).

claim: Blood flow in the brain is tightly coupled to neural activity.
source: Blood flow in the brain is tightly coupled to neural activity.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge.

claim: An increase in neural activity triggers vasodilation to increase delivery of nutrients and clear metabolic waste.
source: Typically, an increase in neural activity triggers vasodilation to increase delivery of nutrients and clear metabolic waste (Chow et al., 2020; Ladecola, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CO2/H+ functions as potent vasodilators in most brain regions to provide support for metabolic activity and maintain brain pH.
source: In most cases, CO2/H+ function as potent vasodilators to provide support for metabolic activity and to maintain brain pH within the narrow range that is conducive to life (Ainslie and Duffin, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CO2/H+ has the opposite effect on vascular tone in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) compared to most brain regions.
source: However, CO2/H+ has the opposite effect on vascular tone in a brainstem region known as the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) (Hawkins et al., 2017; Wenzel et al., 2020), where CO2/H+ is not just metabolic waste to be removed but also functions as a primary stimulus for breathing (Guyenet et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CO2/H+ functions as a primary stimulus for breathing in the RTN.
source: However, CO2/H+ has the opposite effect on vascular tone in a brainstem region known as the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) (Hawkins et al., 2017; Wenzel et al., 2020), where CO2/H+ is not just metabolic waste to be removed but also functions as a primary stimulus for breathing (Guyenet et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Neurons in the RTN are specialized to regulate breathing in response to changes in tissue CO2/H+.
source: Neurons (Guyenet et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2015) and astrocytes (Gourine et al., 2010) in this region are specialized to regulate breathing in response to changes in tissue CO2/H+ (i.e. function as respiratory chemoreceptors)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Astrocytes in the RTN are specialized to regulate breathing in response to changes in tissue CO2/H+.
source: Neurons (Guyenet et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2015) and astrocytes (Gourine et al., 2010) in this region are specialized to regulate breathing in response to changes in tissue CO2/H+ (i.e. function as respiratory chemoreceptors)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Vasoconstriction in the RTN may augment chemoreceptor function by preventing CO2/H+ washout and maintaining the stimulus to respiratory chemoreceptors.
source: and so vasoconstriction may augment this function by preventing CO2/H+ washout and maintaining the stimulus to respiratory chemoreceptors.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on logical inference from the observed vasoconstriction.

claim: RTN chemoreception involves CO2/H+-evoked ATP-purinergic signaling most likely from astrocytes.
source: Previous work showed that RTN chemoreception involves CO2/H+-evoked ATP-purinergic signaling most likely from astrocytes (Gourine et al., 2010; Wenker et al., 2012);
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Endothelial cells in the RTN express P2rx4, P2rx7, and P2ry1,2,6,12-14 receptor transcripts.
source: For example, endothelial cells from each region express ionotropic P2rx4 and P2rx7 and metabotropic P2ry1,2,6,12-14 receptor transcript, albeit at varying levels relative to control (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Smooth muscle cells in the RTN express P2rx1,4 and P2ry2,6,14 receptor transcripts.
source: Also, P2rx1,4 and P2ry2,6,14 receptor transcript were detected in smooth muscle cells from each region and most were under-expressed relative to control (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: P2ry2 transcript was detected at lower levels in RTN endothelial cells compared to control.
source: P2ry2 transcript was detected at lower (−9.2 ± 0.3 log2 fold change, p=0.0013) and higher (6.8 ± 1.5 log2 fold change, p=0.0462) levels compared to control in RTN endothelial and vascular smooth muscle cells, respectively (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data with statistical analysis.

claim: P2ry2 transcript was detected at higher levels in RTN vascular smooth muscle cells compared to control.
source: P2ry2 transcript was detected at lower (−9.2 ± 0.3 log2 fold change, p=0.0013) and higher (6.8 ± 1.5 log2 fold change, p=0.0462) levels compared to control in RTN endothelial and vascular smooth muscle cells, respectively (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data with statistical analysis.

claim: Activation of endothelial P2Y2 receptors favors nitric-oxide-induced vasodilation in other brain regions.
source: This is interesting because in other brain regions activation of endothelial P2Y2 receptors favors nitric-oxide-induced vasodilation (Marrelli, 2001),
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Activation of P2Y2 receptors in vascular smooth muscle cells mediates vasoconstriction.
source: whereas activation of this same receptor in vascular smooth muscle cells mediates vasoconstriction (Brayden et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Exposure to 15% CO2 decreases the diameter of RTN arterioles by −11.2 ± 4.5%.
source: We verified that exposure to CO2/H+ (15% CO2; pH 6.9) under control conditions decreases the diameter of RTN arterioles by −11.2 ± 4.5% (N = 9 vessels),
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Exposure to 15% CO2 dilates arterioles in the caudal NTS by +6.0 ± 2.2%.
source: whereas this same stimulus consistently dilates arterioles in the cNTS (Δ +6.0 ± 2.2%; N = 9 vessels),
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Exposure to 15% CO2 dilates arterioles in the raphe obscurus by +6.5 ± 2.6%.
source: ROb (Δ +6.5 ± 2.6%; N = 11 vessels)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Exposure to 15% CO2 dilates arterioles in the somatosensory cortex by +3.7 ± 0.9%.
source: and somatosensory cortex (Δ +3.7 ± 0.9%; N = 9 vessels) (F3,34=13.49; p<0.0001) (Figure 1Ci–Cii).

claim: CO2/H+-induced constriction of RTN arterioles was eliminated by blockade of P2Y2 receptors with AR-C118925.
source: Consistent with a requisite role of P2Y2 receptors in this response, we found that CO2/H+-induced constriction of RTN arterioles was eliminated by blockade of P2Y2 receptors with AR-C118925 (10 μM) (Δ +0.2 ± 0.3%; N = 6 vessels) (T5 = 1.223; p>0.05) (Figure 1Di–Dii)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Application of a selective P2Y2 receptor agonist (PSB 1114) mimicked CO2/H+-induced constriction of RTN arterioles.
source: and mimicked by application of a selective P2Y2 receptor agonist (PSB 1114; 200 nM) (Δ −2.3 ± 0.7%; N = 11 vessels) (T10 = 3.460; p<0.010) (Figure 1Ei–Eii).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PSB 1114 minimally affects vascular tone in the caudal NTS.
source: As a negative control, we confirmed that PSB 1114 (200 nM) minimally affects vascular tone in the cNTS (Δ −0.05 ± 0.09%; N = 6 vessels; T5 = 0.3898; p>0.05)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PSB 1114 minimally affects vascular tone in the raphe obscurus.
source: and ROb (Δ −0.07 ± 0.19%; N = 7 vessels; T6 = 0.6076; p>0.05) (Figure 1Ei–Eii),
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The response of RTN arterioles to CO2/H+ was retained when neural action potentials were blocked by TTX.
source: We also confirmed that the response of RTN arterioles to CO2/H+ was retained when neural action potentials were blocked by bath application of TTX (0.5 μM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2),
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CO2/H+ constriction of RTN arterioles differs from canonical neurovascular coupling in terms of polarity and dependence on neuronal activity.
source: indicating that CO2/H+ constriction of RTN arterioles differs from canonical neurovascular coupling both in terms of polarity and dependence (or lack thereof) on neuronal activity (Ladecola, 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the TTX experiment and comparison to established knowledge about neurovascular coupling.

claim: The response of RTN arterioles to CO2/H+ was unaffected by 8-phenyltheophylline to block adenosine A1 receptors.
source: Also, despite evidence that extracellular ATP can be rapidly metabolized to adenosine (a potent vasodilator including in the RTN [Hawkins et al., 2017]) the response of RTN arterioles to CO2/H+ was unaffected by 8-phenyltheophylline (8 PT; 10 μM) to block adenosine A1 receptors or sodium metatungstate (POM 1; 100 µM) to inhibit ectonucleotidase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The response of RTN arterioles to CO2/H+ was unaffected by sodium metatungstate (POM 1) to inhibit ectonucleotidase activity.
source: Also, despite evidence that extracellular ATP can be rapidly metabolized to adenosine (a potent vasodilator including in the RTN [Hawkins et al., 2017]) the response of RTN arterioles to CO2/H+ was unaffected by 8-phenyltheophylline (8 PT; 10 μM) to block adenosine A1 receptors or sodium metatungstate (POM 1; 100 µM) to inhibit ectonucleotidase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exposure to CO2/H+ triggers prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) release that may contribute to RTN chemoreception by a mechanism involving EP3 receptors.
source: Furthermore, exposure to CO2/H+ has been shown to trigger prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) release that may contribute to RTN chemoreception by a mechanism involving EP3 receptors (Forsberg et al., 2016);

claim: Bath application of PGE2 (1 µM) decreased RTN arteriole tone by −2.7 ± 0.4%.
source: We found bath application of PGE2 (1 µM) decreased RTN arteriole tone by −2.7 ± 0.4% (T9 = 2.787, p=0.0212, data not shown).

claim: CO2/H+ constriction of RTN vessels was retained in the presence of L-798,106 to block EP3 receptors.

claim: PGE2/EP3 signaling is dispensable for CO2/H+ regulation of arteriole tone in the RTN.
source: suggesting PGE2/EP3 signaling is dispensable for CO2/H+ regulation of arteriole tone in the RTN.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EP3 blocker experiment.

claim: Astrocytes contribute to CO2/H+-induced vasodilation in the cortex.
source: Astrocytes are thought to contribute to CO2/H+induced vasodilation in the cortex (Howarth et al., 2017)

claim: Astrocytes contribute to CO2/H+-induced vasoconstriction in the RTN.
source: and vasoconstriction in the RTN (Hawkins et al., 2017).

source: Consistent with this, we found that exposure to t-ACPD (50 µM), an mGluR agonist widely used to elicit Ca2+ elevations in astrocytes (Howarth et al., 2017), caused constriction of RTN arterioles (Δ −5.9 ± 1.7%; N = 8 vessels)

claim: Exposure to t-ACPD (50 µM) caused dilation of arterioles in the caudal NTS by +7.6 ± 2.5%.

claim: Increasing end-expiratory CO2 to 9–10% corresponds with an arterial pH of 7.2 pH units.
source: Consistent with our slice data, we found under saline control conditions that increasing end-expiratory CO2 to 9–10%, which corresponds with an arterial pH of 7.2 pH units (Guyenet et al., 2005),

claim: Increasing inspired CO2 to 9-10% constricted VMS vessels by −7.8 ± 0.7% under saline control conditions.
source: constricted VMS vessels by −7.8 ± 0.7% (p=0.01, N = 7 animals) (Figure 2A).

claim: When P2Y2-receptors are blocked by application of AR-C118925, increasing inspired CO2 resulted in a vasodilation of 5.2 ± 0.9%.
source: However, when P2Y2-receptors are blocked by application of AR-C118925 (10 µM) to the VMS, increasing inspired CO2 resulted in a vasodilation of 5.2 ± 0.9% (Figure 2A) (p=0.05; N = 7 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the absence of functional P2Y2 receptors, RTN vessels respond to CO2/H+ in a manner similar to other brain regions.
source: Thus, in the absence of functional P2Y2 receptors, RTN vessels respond to CO2/H+ in a manner similar to other brain regions.

claim: Activation of P2Y2 receptors by application of PSB1114 (100 µM) to the VMS constricted vessels in the region of the RTN by −6.3 ± 0.9%.
source: Also consistent with our slice data, we found that activation of P2Y2 receptors by application of PSB1114 (100 µM) to the VMS constricted vessels in the region of the RTN by −6.3 ± 0.9% (p=0.05, N = 7 animals) (Figure 2B).

claim: VMS application of AR-C118925 minimally affected the CO2/H+ apneic threshold.
source: We found that VMS application of AR-C118925 (1 mM) minimally affected the CO2/H+ apneic threshold (3.3 ± 0.4% vs. saline: 3.1 ± 0.5%) (p>0.05; two-way RM ANOVA; N = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: At high levels of CO2 (9–10% etCO2) AR-C118925 decreased intercostal EMG amplitude by 23 ± 5%.
source: However, at high levels of CO2 (9–10% etCO2) AR-C118925 decreased intercostal EMG amplitude by 23 ± 5% (F2,74 = 69.83; p=0.021; N = 7 animals) (Figure 2C,E),
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,E.

claim: VMS application of PSB1114 (100 µM) while holding etCO2 constant at 5% increased intercostal EMG amplitude by 20 ± 3%.
source: Conversely, VMS application of PSB1114 (100 µM) while holding etCO2 constant at 5% increased intercostal EMG amplitude by 20 ± 3% (F2,74 = 96.14; p=0.02; N = 7 animals) (Figure 2D,H),

claim: P2Y2 dependent vasoconstriction in the RTN contributes to the drive to breathe.
source: These results indicate that P2Y2 dependent vasoconstriction in the RTN contributes to the drive to breathe.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined results of pharmacological manipulations on ventilation.

claim: Vasodilation in the caudal NTS and raphe obscurus should buffer tissue CO2/H+ and limit contributions of these regions to respiratory output.
source: If the mechanism underlying vascular control of RTN chemoreception involves maintenance of tissue CO2/H+ levels, then by this same logic, vasodilation in the cNTS and ROb should buffer tissue CO2/H+ and limit contributions of these regions to respiratory output.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Over-activation of the CO2/H+ chemoreflex is thought to cause unstable periodic breathing.
source: Such a braking mechanism may be important for stabilizing breathing since over-activation of the CO2/H+ chemoreflex is thought to cause unstable periodic breathing (Cherniack and Longobardo, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Injections of U46619 (1 μM) into the caudal NTS and raphe obscurus resulted in unstable breathing with frequent bouts of hyperventilation followed by apnea.
source: We found that injections of U46619 (1 μM) into the cNTS alone caused an increase in breathing frequency but together with the ROb resulted in unstable breathing as evidenced by frequent bouts of hyperventilation followed by apnea (Figure 3A) (1.2 ± 0.6, vs. saline: 0.4 ± 0.2 apneas/min; p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Application of U46619 into the caudal NTS and raphe obscurus lowered the CO2 apneic threshold from 3.2 ± 0.3% to 2.1 ± 0.1%.
source: Consistent with increased chemoreceptor drive, we found that application of U46619 into these regions lowered the CO2 apneic threshold from 3.2 ± 0.3% to 2.1 ± 0.1% (p<0.05; two-way RM ANOVA; N = 7) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Injection of U46619 (1 μM) into the caudal NTS increased systemic blood pressure.
source: Also, consistent with previous work (Yalcin and Savci, 2004), we found that injection of U46619 (1 μM) into the cNTS also increased systemic blood pressure (127 ± 11, vs. saline: 98 ± 4 mmHg), (F3,65 = 77.62; p<0.01, data not shown),
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (not shown in figures) and citation to prior work.

claim: Application of U46619 into the raphe obscurus alone had negligible effects on cardiorespiratory output.
source: whereas, application of this drug into the ROb alone had negligible effects on cardiorespiratory output.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: CO2/H+ induced vasoconstriction in the RTN serves to enhance chemoreceptor drive.
source: Together, these results show that CO2/H+ induced vasoconstriction in the RTN serves to enhance chemoreceptor drive,
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental results.
